new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and quantity-driven: any syllable with a long vowel carries stress; if two adjacent syllables both have long vowels, the second (rightmost) one is stressed. The source gives no default position for words containing only short vowels (Das notes elsewhere, p.11, that long vowels never occur word-finally; Mahapatra 1979 and Steever 1998 state that long vowels occur only in the word-initial syllable, which would make long-vowel stress effectively initial in native vocabulary).
new_statements.exceptions: None; only the two-long-vowel case is treated (last one stressed).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement in the phonology chapter, given alongside sections on transition features (word juncture) and sentence-final intonation contours (1.4-1.5); examples are citation forms. Description based on fieldwork in the Santal Parganas (Hiranpur, Banjhi, Simul Kundi).
new_statements.identity_note: Das 1973 describes 'Malto' from fieldwork in the southern Santal Parganas (Pahariya schools at Hiranpur and Banjhi, villagers of Simul Kundi, Pakur/Amrapara area) and identifies the Sauriya Pahariya as the Malto speakers; he does not distinguish Sauria vs Kumarbhag Paharia dialects, so the statement is for Malto generally rather than certified Sauria Paharia [mjt] as opposed to Kumarbhag Paharia [kmj]. Mahapatra 1976/1979/1987 (silent on stress) take the Dravidian-speaking Malpaharia variety as reference dialect with Sawria and Kumarbhag variants noted; Puttaswamy 2009 and Bokade 2021 (also silent) are explicitly Sauriya/Sauria Pahariya.

tone.quote: Not much is known about the word stress and intonation of Malto, except that some forms have unique pitch peaks, e.g. the negative imperative such as lap-óma {eat-NG.IMP} ‘don’t eat’, or the optative such as ɖoːk-aːndér {stay-OP.3PL} ‘let them stay’, but they might as well be attributed to intonational pitch contour. … A long vowel in the initial syllable is often shortened when the second syllable has prominence such as length and high pitch; for example, eːk-a {go-IMP} ‘let’s go!’ is actually pronounced [eˈkaː].
tone.summary: No tone system described; the grammar only notes pitch peaks on a few verb forms (negative imperative, optative), which it says may be intonational, and high prominence of initial syllables.
tone.says: No tone system described; the grammar only notes pitch peaks on a few verb forms (negative imperative, optative), which it says may be intonational, and high prominence of initial syllables.
